I used to think my iPhone setup was fine until I started changing it. 

Most people just stick with the default apps. They work, but they rarely feel personal or fast. I spent the last few months replacing the basics with tools that actually respect my time. 

Here are five apps that changed how I use my device daily:

1. Arc Search. It does the browsing for me. Instead of giving me a list of links, it summarizes the answer directly. It saves me from clicking through SEO-heavy sites just to find one data point.

2. Raycast. This is a on the Mac side, but the mobile integration is solid. I use it to launch apps and run scripts without touching the home screen. 

3. Obsidian. I stopped using standard notes apps. Obsidian feels like a brain dump that I can actually search through later. It handles my project ideas for Prettiva and STRAYED without any clutter.

4. Proton Mail. Privacy matters more when you are building things. It is simple, fast, and does not try to track my every move.

5. Dark Noise. I cannot work in silence, and this app has the best background sounds. It helps me focus when I am coding in a noisy cafe in Bangalore.

None of these apps are complicated. They just do one thing and they do it well. 

I am curious about your workflow. What is the one app you downloaded that stayed on your home screen for more than a year?

#productivity #ios #minimalism #tech

5 apps on my phone that I genuinely use all the time, but barely see anyone talking about.

As someone who spends a lot of time studying, building things, and working on projects, I've ended up collecting a bunch of very specific apps that solve very specific problems.

These 5 have become part of my daily workflow:

1. SwiftSlate

This one is probably my favourite.

Instead of copying text into ChatGPT every time I want to fix or rewrite something, I can do it directly wherever I'm typing.

For example:

"?fix" → fixes the grammar
"?formal" → makes it formal

So if I'm writing an email and want it to sound more professional, I just add "?formal" and it's done.

No copying. No switching apps. No opening ChatGPT.

https://github.com/Musheer360/SwiftSlate

2. Wispr Flow

I've been using this one constantly.

Sometimes I just don't want to type.

I can talk to my phone normally, even if what I'm saying is messy or full of pauses, and Wispr Flow turns it into properly formatted text.

It removes the gibberish, fixes the sentences, adds punctuation, and actually makes sense of what I'm trying to say.

I use it for messages, emails, LinkedIn posts, prompts, and even while coding.

I'm actually using it to write this post right now. 😂

https://wisprflow.ai/

3. Mark

If you're like me, your gallery is probably full of screenshots you took for 5 minutes and never needed again.

Mark fixes that.

Whenever I take a screenshot, it gives me the option to automatically delete it after a set amount of time.

When I'm building a website or an app, I'll often take a screenshot, set it to delete after 15 minutes, share it to my laptop, and forget about it.

Then it disappears automatically.

No more hundreds of random screenshots clogging up my gallery.

https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.markOne.ss_app

4. Essentials

This is one of those Android apps where you keep discovering another useful feature.

It has things like Private DNS controls, battery information, automation, USB debugging controls, and a ton of other system-level tools.

The feature I use the most is the automation around developer and accessibility settings.

Because I use accessibility services and USB debugging for development, some banking and UPI apps don't let me use them while those settings are enabled.

Essentials lets me automatically handle those settings when I open certain apps, so I don't have to keep manually turning everything off and back on.

It's a very small thing, but it saves me a lot of frustration.

https://sameerasw.com/essentials

5. Droplert

I only discovered this one recently, but I already love it.
I use it to track things I want to buy and get notified when the price drops.

What's really cool is that it can track prices from practically any website. I can paste a product link, choose the price I want to track, and let it do the checking for me. It can also show price history and let me set a target price.

I've been using it for everything from products and gifts to things like subscriptions and online services.

And honestly, I had to mention it because the app itself is just really well designed.

https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.shahzaman.pricetracker

These aren't necessarily the most popular apps on my phone.

They're just apps that solve small problems really well, and those are often the apps I end up using the most.

What's one underrated app on your phone that you think more people should know about?

#Android #Productivity #Apps #DeveloperTools #Technology #StudentLife

I almost quit Karate after 8 years.

I started learning Karate when I was around 10 years old.

For years, every Tuesday and Thursday, I'd show up to training. I went from a white belt, all the way to brown.

But somewhere along the way, I started losing interest.

As I got older, Karate just didn't feel as exciting anymore. I wanted to stop.

But my parents encouraged me to keep going.

And I remember thinking:

"If I stop now, what do I have to show for all these years?"

So I kept going.

For another year and a half, I pushed through. I eventually switched to a much more intensive training session once a week and started putting in more effort than I had before.

After around 10 years of training, I finally earned my Black Belt. 🥋

Looking back, getting the Black Belt wasn't the hardest part.

The hardest part was continuing when I didn't want to.

Karate taught me something I've found myself using in almost everything I do now:

Motivation gets you started. Commitment keeps you going.

Sometimes you don't need to love what you're doing every day.

You just need to keep showing up.

You don't need to know how you're going to achieve your goal. You just need to believe it's possible.

I've started to realize this more and more over the years.

Before starting my clothing brands, I knew almost nothing about running a business.

I didn't know how to find manufacturers. I didn't know how to source products. I didn't know how to build a brand.

I just had an idea and wanted to see if I could make it work.

When we started working on STRAYED, I didn't even know how I was going to build the website from scratch with the limitations we had.

So I figured it out.

With Prettiva & Co., we initially tried Amazon because it seemed like the easiest way to get started. Eventually, we realized it wasn't the right fit for what we wanted to do.

So we looked for other options.

We tried things, changed our approach, found solutions that worked for us, and kept moving.

And that's probably one of the biggest things I've learned from all of this:

You don't always need the answer before you start.

Sometimes you just need a goal big enough that you're willing to figure out the rest along the way.

There will be things you don't know.
There will be things that don't work.
There will be times when you have no idea what to do next.

But there's almost always another way forward.

It might take weeks. It might take months.

But if you keep looking, keep learning, and don't give up, you'll eventually find a way.

So dream big.

Don't limit your goals based on what you think is possible today.

Set the goal first.

Figure out the how along the way.
